Business Models

SmartUp Foundations Course - Lecture 4

Given June 2nd, 2024 by Yonatan Stern


We are on to lecture four, and this one is on a different subject altogether, which is business models. I apologize in advance, there will be a lot of spreadsheets all over, because a business model is with spreadsheets, but I tried as much as possible to make them easy to follow and understand. I'll start with the usual introduction. Myself, Libby is on vacation, so don't look for her. And again, what we try to do here is a program to teach the profession of building successful companies. And as I said many times, building a company is a profession like any other profession, which means you graduate from university, you might have some clues about the idea, but real life looks very different than all the people with companies in their head.

It is very different than what you might be studying in school, and so we teach it. First of all, we said building successful companies, and we have a definition of what is a successful company, and we're going to dive into that definition at length during this meeting. So there are three criteria, three pillars of the idea. One is the company has to strive for profitability from day one. That's the target of the company, produce money, be cash flow positive. That's number one. Number two, it has to be fast growing. And number three, it has to have a modest investment, because as I will describe later on, this whole notion of how you do the financing and for people like you that might be very interesting as angel investors.

The methodology we are showing in here takes into account that the money you get has to go back to the investor. So when you reach profitability, you have to start paying back the investment you got.

And we do also workshops, which is a few companies sitting together, two, three companies on a subject like how do you do a brand, and then we sit down specifically with those companies. And obviously, as you can see, the residency picture we have in here, because it takes a long time to build the company, and we found that at every step of the way, there are questions, and we have regular meetings with our companies — regular, I mean, once a week, once every two weeks, depending on the status of the company. And as Maury mentioned to me, they gave me homework now for a meeting that they have. Okay, what is the language of business? So "mathematics is the language in which God has written the universe." That said Galileo Galilei at the turn of the 17th century.

And what he did is he was the first to write an equation in physics. You can see it on the right, the famous experiment of dropping a heavy body and a small body and showing and proving that they reached the ground at the same time. By the way, he didn't do it this way, because it was too fast to measure. He did it on an inclined plane where he rolled two balls, but the concept was the same. So what is the language of business? We talked about it — money, but this time I added a little more. So when we say money, we need to build a model that can calculate the money. And every decision that we want to make has to be converted or expressed in the model in monetary terms.

If we raise the price, if we lower the price, if we hire more people, if we hire less people, if we do branding first or branding later, all of these have to be expressed in the model so that you can measure the impact that they have. So let's start with a few questions. Why profitable, fast-growing, and modest investment? So I'll answer. What's the difference between a company that generates a million dollars a year and a company that loses a million dollars a year? I'd like to ask this question because the answers are not the same. It's not two million dollars. Those who answer two million dollars should start at grade one. So if you lose a million dollars a year and you have five million dollars in the bank, you know you have five years to live. It's that simple.

So you either raise more money, get diluted, have a fight with your investors and whatever, or you just run out of money and you shut down the business. Those of you who have some experience, I have seen it many times — I see it on the smiles on the faces in here, all the people who encountered this dilemma. So don't lose a million dollars a year. Don't lose a dollar a year. Make money all the time. A company that generates a million dollars a year lives the infinite game. Last time, I think two times before, I spoke about what is the infinite game. The infinite game is: why do you build a company?

Do you build it with a target of winning, of reaching somewhere, or because that's what you want to do and you enjoy every day of the week and the people around you are excited and you think about it as that's what you want to do in your life, period. That's the infinite game. You build things or you tend to your garden, which I now do, because it's fun and I like the flowers and that's it. So a company that makes money — you can thrive and you can grow and you don't owe anybody anything. And you have figured out a successful business model. You don't make money by mistake. So somehow you figured out how to sell your product or service or whatever at a price that is way above the cost and you make money.

So that's already a huge check mark on what you do. Now you have time and resources to pursue other worthy purposes. For example, I founded CardScan, I built Zoom, from Zoom I built Bezo, then I built this — all of it is one coming out of the other because when you generate money, you're a master of your life and you can do whatever you want and that's a lot of fun, that's the infinite game. So I want to wish on all of you — get there and do whatever you want. You have the independence to do whatever you want because you don't need permission from anybody, you can pay the bills, you can go to any restaurant you want or even walk on the beach. And the last item is really important. A profitable company is much easier to sell than a losing company.

And the reason — there are two reasons for that. Reason number one, the buyer knows you are not in a stress to sell. So you can negotiate with a smile on your face and you have all the time in the world, meanwhile you generate money that sits in the bank and everybody wants to put their hand on the money sitting in your bank or on the machine that generates that money. So a company that generates money has a floor on the price people are willing to pay for it. Usually it's times 20, times 15, times 30, depends. So if you generate a million dollars a year, you're probably worth anywhere between 20 and 30 million. It's that simple.

And then, of course, you will get all the money above it based on what you do and how important it is and all the other stuff. So that's very important. So now that you are convinced to make money, why do you need to grow fast? What's wrong with sitting idle and making enough money to pay for lunch and your kids and that's about it? So first and foremost, it's the ability to pay the investors back. Maybe I'm a bizarre creature that thinks that when people give you money, they want it back. And they want it back with a pretty high certainty. "One out of ten companies succeed" is, excuse me for the term, stupid. You should think about it — when somebody gave me a million dollars, that's a lot of money, I need to return that money.

Your behavior becomes very different when you think like that. So start thinking like that because it will help your life. And when you grow fast, you get a compounded growth in the value of the company. So I explained to you what that means. I said before, if you make a million dollars a year, people can calculate your worth anywhere between 20 and 30 million. But what if the year before, you did half a million and you have very good plans to do three million next year because you are growing fast, you built the engine? Then clearly you are not going to sell the company on what you are doing now. You will tell the buyer, "Listen, next year we're going to do three million, I want a multiple of three." But why only next year?

"I will be five million dollars in profits two years from now." So you have tremendous power to negotiate the value of your company. Companies that grow fast attract tremendous attention. So grow fast, you can do that. A company that doesn't grow fast is just not interesting for me, but I'll leave it for you. And why modest investment? Because it's much easier to raise small amounts of money, not always from VCs — but I think if you haven't noticed my opinion about how VCs operate, then you don't listen. You have many more sources for financing. Somebody here asked me how I started — it was with $50,000 that somebody gave me just to build something, and he also recommended an engineer. That's how the company started.

So you can start, and if you use the money wisely, you can use that to build more and more, and you don't need a lot of money. Second, which we're going to talk about later, founders can keep much bigger ownership, because money doesn't come for free. When you raise money, somebody wants it back. VCs usually want it in terms of ownership of the company, so you get diluted. What we're going to do later in this meeting — we had last time, sorry. Two parts. We're very fortunate to have here Yael Levinson. Can you please raise your hand? He's also a mentor at SmartUp, and he has a very interesting story about the company he built.

I will not steal your thunder, and we will have a very interesting piece of humor at the end, so those of you who want to leave before the end will miss it. And it's based on your assumptions. Each column represents a time, usually a month, because that's how we all are used to working. Sometimes as we move out into the future, sometimes annually if we move really far out.

But I think it's very important to be down to a month because a month is long enough. And each row is an item, so you have a spreadsheet, okay? Each column is months, and each row is something. We will see it later on. And the business model allows us — remember, you have to put all your assumptions in. It's a good way to analyze a lot of your assumptions and parameters, like your pricing, payment terms, hiring, people, whatever it is. Very, very powerful tool. We'll see some examples as I go on. Now, if you build the model correctly, you can use it later on as a tool to track what you're doing. So you kind of build the model, you think you understand what you're doing, and then you start hiring people, try to sell, and so forth.

For example, number one is, I want to sell computers, it costs me money to produce a computer. I sell shoes, I need to put the price of the pair of shoes before I sell them. With customer acquisition cost using Google Ads, for example, it's relatively straightforward. Why? Because you can track the entire process. With a billboard, you have no idea who saw the billboard, who bought, whatever. So nowadays, because a lot of things are done on the web, it's relatively easy to follow the customer acquisition cost. And then you have sales cost. If you have a sales group and you want them to sell, you pay them a salary. Many times you pay them commissions. And you know how much they sold.

So if they sold $100,000 in a month, and they cost you $20,000 that month, then 20% of your sale is cost of sales. Now, by the way, I'm not trying to be very accurate in here. What that means is you have a company, so you have people, you have management, you have space, you have cloud computing, you have operations. And they're kind of static in the sense that you cannot hire and fire people every week based on whether you use them or not. You cannot break your office lease over the weekend and get the money back.

So these are fixed expenses, but I don't use the term "fixed" because it has a totally different meaning in accounting. So I don't want to confuse it. But essentially anything that is not variable, directly depending on the sale, I put it under this. It's just a whole section of all your expenses. And then there are one-time big expenses. You build a lab, you take McKinsey to do some consulting for you for half a million dollars, whatever it is. But the most important thing is that the smart business model is an operational cash flow model. It is not an accounting P&L, standard P&L. Why cash? Mainly because when people work for you, they want to get paid.

So they don't really care about your P&L, they don't care about your assets, they don't care about anything, they just want to get paid by the end of the month. So cash is king. This is a cash model, not a P&L model, for those of you who know the difference. Okay, every model is based on assumptions like time to market, pricing, customer acquisition cost, all of these. Do we want to have the price at $1,000, $1,500, $500, and so forth and so on. There are elements that are tied to one another. For example, price elasticity.

The reason I bring it up here is not just to guess — yes, you need to guess — but when I said branding first, I wanted to also point out that a lot of the things you can do is test these things. You will feel much more comfortable taking $2,000 instead of $1,000 in your model if in your test you saw that instead of 10 people responding to the $1,000, 8 people responded to the $2,000. For those of you who are very quick with math, 10 times $1,000 is $10,000. 8 times $2,000 is $16,000. It's $6,000 more.

How are you going to do that? He says, well, currently we sell the product for $249. I'm going to raise it to $259. I don't think anybody will notice. And he did it. And he generated another million dollars. So yes, you want to charge as high as possible as long as you make more money along the way. So this correlation between price and number of customers is critical. For the purpose of the model, it is to test different values. This is what I'm telling you. This lecture explores the foundational principles of business models, emphasizing that building a successful company is a learnable profession grounded in rigorous methodology rather than intuition. The instructor, Yonatan Stern, defines a successful company through three pillars: striving for profitability from day one, achieving fast growth, and operating with modest investment. He draws a vivid contrast between a company earning a million dollars annually and one losing the same amount — the profitable company plays "the infinite game," enjoying independence, longevity, and the freedom to pursue new ventures, while the unprofitable one faces a countdown to extinction.

Central to the lecture is the idea that money is the language of business, just as mathematics is the language of the universe. Every strategic decision — pricing, hiring, branding timing — must be expressed in a financial model so its impact can be measured. The business model serves as the analytical backbone of the company, translating assumptions into numbers and enabling founders to test whether their venture is viable before committing significant resources.

A key practical insight is the importance of testing assumptions early and cheaply. Rather than building a product first and hoping customers will come, founders should validate price sensitivity and demand through techniques like A/B/C testing on landing pages, measuring what potential customers are willing to pay before development begins. If the numbers do not converge — if production costs exceed what customers will pay — there is no business model, and founders should pivot before wasting time and capital. The lecture also touches on pricing strategy for physical products, recommending a three-to-five-times markup over production cost as a rule of thumb, and illustrates how even small price increases can dramatically multiply profit margins.

A guest speaker, Yael, shares the story of Iridize, a software company that competed with WalkMe and was eventually acquired by Oracle. Her narrative reinforces the lecture's themes of perseverance through the emotional highs and lows of entrepreneurship. The session concludes with a discussion of creative go-to-market strategies, including using TikTok's algorithm to test product-market fit at minimal cost, and the importance of listening to market signals rather than theorizing in isolation. Throughout, the lecture reinforces that disciplined financial modeling and early market validation are the true engines of entrepreneurial success.
